ming-dynasty.name: Ming dynasty
ming-dynasty.summary: China's last dynasty ruled by the Han majority, reigning 1368 to 1644 after the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty's fall, founded by the Hongwu Emperor.

columbian-exchange.name: Columbian exchange
columbian-exchange.summary: The widespread transfer of plants, animals and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia beginning in the late 15th century, named for Christopher Columbus.

kangxi-emperor.name: Kangxi Emperor
kangxi-emperor.summary: Third emperor of China's Qing dynasty (1654–1722), whose 61-year reign is the longest in Chinese history, who suppressed a revolt and expanded the empire into Taiwan and Tibet.

qing-dynasty.name: Qing dynasty
qing-dynasty.summary: Manchu-led imperial dynasty of China from 1644 to 1912, the last imperial dynasty, which at its height controlled more territory than any other dynasty in Chinese history.

manchu-han-imperial-feast.name: Manchu–Han Imperial Feast
manchu-han-imperial-feast.summary: A grand banquet style blending Manchu and Han Chinese cuisine that developed during the Qing dynasty (1644–1912) and became widely imitated in restaurants by the 19th century.

qianlong-emperor.name: Qianlong Emperor
qianlong-emperor.summary: Fifth emperor of the Qing dynasty, reigning from 1735 to 1796, who expanded Chinese territory into Inner Asia, including conquering Xinjiang from the Dzungar Khanate.

imperial-household-department.name: Imperial Household Department
imperial-household-department.summary: Qing dynasty institution that managed the internal affairs of the imperial family and inner palace, and also handled trade, ceremonies, and relations with Tibet and Mongolia.

century-egg.name: Century egg
century-egg.summary: A Chinese dish of duck, chicken or quail eggs preserved for weeks or months in clay, ash, salt and lime, which darkens the yolk and turns the white into a jelly-like texture.

song-dynasty.name: Song dynasty
song-dynasty.summary: Imperial Chinese dynasty that ruled from 960 to 1279, later split into a northern and southern period after losing northern China to the Jurchen Jin dynasty, before its conquest by the Mongols.

hunan-cuisine.name: Hunan Cuisine
hunan-cuisine.summary: One of China's Eight Great Traditions of cooking, from the Xiang River region, known for hot, spicy flavors and techniques like stewing, frying and smoking, though only about a fifth of dishes actually use chili.

mala-seasoning.name: Mala
mala-seasoning.summary: Numbing and spicy Sichuan seasoning made from Sichuan peppercorn and chili, often simmered into a sauce and central to Sichuan and Chongqing cuisine.

sichuan-pepper.name: Sichuan pepper
sichuan-pepper.summary: Spice made from the dried outer shell of Zanthoxylum fruit, used in Sichuan cuisine for a tingling, numbing effect, and unrelated to black or chili pepper despite the name.

chen-jiru.name: Chen Jiru
chen-jiru.summary: A Chinese landscape painter, calligrapher and essayist of the Ming dynasty (1558 to 1639), who wrote on tea, pottery and diet, including Tea Talks (1595), and was known for short literary essays.

fang-yizhi.name: Fang Yizhi
fang-yizhi.summary: Chinese politician, polymath monk, and author of scientific textbooks in the late Ming and early Qing dynasties (1611–1671).

chizhou.name: Chizhou
chizhou.summary: A city in Anhui province, China, home to Mount Jiuhua, one of Chinese Buddhism's four sacred mountains.

wen-zhengming.name: Wen Zhengming
wen-zhengming.summary: Chinese painter, calligrapher and poet of the Ming dynasty (1470 to 1559), regarded as one of the Four Masters of Ming painting.

dong-qichang.name: Dong Qichang
dong-qichang.summary: Chinese art theorist, calligrapher, painter and politician of the late Ming dynasty (1555–1636).

famille-rose.name: Famille rose
famille-rose.summary: A style of Chinese porcelain decoration dominated by pink overglaze enamel, introduced in the 18th century and reaching its finest quality during the Qianlong period.

manual-of-the-mustard-seed-garden.name: Manual of the Mustard Seed Garden
manual-of-the-mustard-seed-garden.summary: A printed manual of Chinese painting compiled in the early Qing dynasty and first published in 1679, used to teach generations of Chinese and Japanese painters and notable for early color printing.
manual-of-the-mustard-seed-garden.source_title: Manual of the Mustard Seed Garden

emin-minaret.name: Emin Minaret
emin-minaret.summary: China's tallest minaret at 44 meters, built in Turfan in 1777-78 and named for the Uyghur leader Emin Khoja, blending Islamic and local Uyghur architectural styles.

turpan.name: Turpan
turpan.summary: A prefecture-level city in Xinjiang, China, with a population of about 694,000, whose historical center shifted over time from Yar-Khoto to Qocho and finally to Turpan itself.

four-wangs.name: Four Wangs
four-wangs.summary: Four 17th-century Chinese landscape painters, all surnamed Wang, renowned in the Qing dynasty's Orthodox school of shan shui painting.

wang-shimin.name: Wang Shimin
wang-shimin.summary: A Chinese landscape painter (c. 1592–1680) of the late Ming and early Qing dynasties, ranked among the influential 'Four Wangs' and 'Six Masters' for recreating the brushwork of past masters.

bada-shanren.name: Bada Shanren
bada-shanren.summary: A Chinese painter, calligrapher and poet (1626–1705), born a Ming prince, who spent thirty years as a Buddhist monk before a late career often reflecting on the Ming dynasty's fall.

shitao.name: Shitao
shitao.summary: A Chinese Buddhist monk, calligrapher and landscape painter (1642–1707), born into the Ming imperial clan, who took monastic vows after the Ming dynasty's fall and later converted to Daoism.

fran-ois-xavier-d-entrecolles.name: François Xavier d'Entrecolles
fran-ois-xavier-d-entrecolles.summary: French Jesuit priest (1664–1741) who learned Chinese porcelain-making at Jingdezhen and published his findings in a 1712 letter studied across Europe.

jingdezhen.name: Jingdezhen
jingdezhen.summary: City in Jiangxi province known as China's 'Porcelain Capital,' having produced the country's finest ceramics for over 1,000 years.

petuntse.name: Petuntse
petuntse.summary: A historic Chinese term for feldspathic rock crushed into 'little white bricks' and mixed with kaolin as a key raw material for porcelain.

wang-yuanqi.name: Wang Yuanqi
wang-yuanqi.summary: Chinese landscape painter of the Qing dynasty (1642–1715), one of the 'Four Wangs' among the Six Masters, who served as a court official and curator of the imperial art collection under the Kangxi Emperor.

giuseppe-tucci.name: Giuseppe Tucci
giuseppe-tucci.summary: An Italian orientalist and scholar (1894–1984) specializing in Tibetan culture and Buddhism, considered one of the founders of Buddhist studies.

tuen-mun.name: Tuen Mun
tuen-mun.summary: Area near the New Territories of Hong Kong, one of the region's earliest settlements dating to the Neolithic period; site of naval clashes between Ming China and Portugal in 1521–1522.

jiajing-emperor.name: Jiajing Emperor
jiajing-emperor.summary: 12th emperor of China's Ming dynasty (1507–1567), reigning 1521 to 1567; his early reign was dominated by the Great Rites Controversy, and he later governed from a palace complex outside the Forbidden City devoted to Taoist practice.

wokou.name: Wokou
wokou.summary: Pirates known as 'Japanese pirates' or 'dwarf pirates' who raided the coasts of China and Korea from the 13th to 17th centuries, drawn from various East Asian peoples.

penghu.name: Penghu
penghu.summary: An archipelago of 90 islands in the Taiwan Strait, settled by Chinese people since the Song dynasty and briefly occupied by the Dutch and French before later Japanese and Republic of China rule.

battle-of-liaoluo-bay.name: Battle of Liaoluo Bay
battle-of-liaoluo-bay.summary: 1633 naval battle off Fujian, China, in which Ming forces defeated the Dutch East India Company, the largest Sino-European naval clash before the Opium Wars.

koxinga.name: Koxinga
koxinga.summary: Southern Ming general (1624–1662) who resisted the Qing conquest of China and drove the Dutch from Taiwan in 1662, founding the Kingdom of Tungning.

miao-rebellion-1795-1806.name: Miao Rebellion
miao-rebellion-1795-1806.summary: An anti-Qing uprising in Hunan and Guizhou provinces from 1795 to 1806, fueled by tensions between local peoples and Han Chinese settlers, bloodily suppressed by the Qing.

white-lotus-rebellion.name: White Lotus Rebellion
white-lotus-rebellion.summary: A rebellion (1794-1804) by followers of a millenarian Buddhist movement against the Qing dynasty in China, crushed after eight years but marking a sharp decline in Qing power.

classical-chinese.name: Literary Chinese
classical-chinese.summary: The written literary form of Chinese used from the 5th century BCE and adopted across Vietnam, Korea, Japan and the Ryukyus as a shared language of scholarship and administration until the early 20th century.

jonathan-chaves.name: Jonathan Chaves
jonathan-chaves.summary: American sinologist (born 1943) and professor of Chinese language and literature at George Washington University, known as a translator of classical Chinese poetry.

shen-zhou.name: Shen Zhou
shen-zhou.summary: Chinese painter of the Ming dynasty (1427–1509) who lived reclusively after retiring, contributing to the individualist Wu School of Chinese art.

tang-yin.name: Tang Yin
tang-yin.summary: Chinese painter, calligrapher and poet of the Ming dynasty (1470–1524), ranked among the 'Four Masters of Ming dynasty' and the 'Four Literary Masters of the Wuzhong Region'.

yun-shouping.name: Yun Shouping
yun-shouping.summary: Chinese calligrapher and painter (1633–1690), a major artist of the early Qing dynasty and one of the 'Six Masters' of the period.

chongzhen-emperor.name: Chongzhen Emperor
chongzhen-emperor.summary: Last emperor of China's Ming dynasty, reigning 1627 to 1644, who fought peasant rebellions and Manchu incursions and took his own life when rebels captured Beijing.

li-zicheng.name: Li Zicheng
li-zicheng.summary: Chinese rebel leader (1606–1645) who overthrew the Ming dynasty in 1644 and briefly reigned as emperor of the Shun dynasty before his defeat by Qing forces.

wu-weiye.name: Wu Weiye
wu-weiye.summary: Chinese poet and politician (1609-1671) who lived through the Ming-Qing transition and was known as one of the Three Masters of Jiangdong for his ci poetry and verse on current events.

qian-qianyi.name: Qian Qianyi
qian-qianyi.summary: Chinese historian, poet and politician of the late Ming dynasty (1582–1664), one of the Three Masters of Jiangdong alongside Wu Weiye and Gong Dingzi.

gong-dingzi.name: Gong Dingzi
gong-dingzi.summary: Chinese poet and politician (1615–1673) who served under the Ming, the short-lived Dashun regime, and then the Qing dynasty; grouped with Wu Weiye and Qian Qianyi as the Three Masters of Jiangdong.

complete-tang-poems.name: Complete Tang Poems
complete-tang-poems.summary: The largest collection of Tang dynasty poetry, about 49,000 poems by over 2,200 poets, commissioned in 1705 under the Qing Kangxi Emperor.

chinese-opera.name: Chinese opera
chinese-opera.summary: A form of Chinese musical theatre combining music, dance, martial arts, acrobatics and elaborate costume and make-up, reaching mature form in the 13th century; Peking opera is its best-known modern branch.

dong-xiaowan.name: Dong Xiaowan
dong-xiaowan.summary: Chinese courtesan and poet (1624–1651) celebrated for her beauty and artistic talents, counted among the Eight Beauties of Qinhuai.

liu-rushi.name: Liu Rushi
liu-rushi.summary: A Chinese courtesan, poet and writer of the late Ming and early Qing dynasties (1618-1664), one of the 'Eight Beauties of Qinhuai', later revered for her loyalty to her husband and to the Ming.

three-hundred-tang-poems.name: Three Hundred Tang Poems
three-hundred-tang-poems.summary: An anthology of over 300 Tang dynasty poems compiled around 1763, long used to teach Chinese children to read and write.

classic-of-poetry.name: Classic of Poetry
classic-of-poetry.summary: The oldest surviving collection of Chinese poetry, comprising 305 works from the 11th to 7th centuries BC and traditionally said to be edited by Confucius.

joseph-needham.name: Joseph Needham
joseph-needham.summary: British biochemist, historian of science and sinologist known for the multivolume Science and Civilisation in China and for posing the "Needham Question" about China's loss of scientific leadership.

four-great-inventions.name: Four Great Inventions
four-great-inventions.summary: The compass, gunpowder, papermaking and printing—four Chinese inventions celebrated as symbols of ancient China's advanced technology.

francis-bacon.name: Francis Bacon
francis-bacon.summary: English philosopher and statesman (1561–1626) who served as Attorney General and Lord Chancellor under King James I; called the father of empiricism for arguing science should rest on careful observation and inductive reasoning.

nathan-sivin.name: Nathan Sivin
nathan-sivin.summary: An American historian of science (1931–2022) who studied Chinese science, medicine and philosophy and helped establish their scholarly study in the West.

hong-taiji.name: Hong Taiji
hong-taiji.summary: Second khan of the Later Jin dynasty and founding emperor of the Qing dynasty (1592 to 1643), who conquered Inner Mongolia and Manchuria and made Korea a Qing tributary.

later-jin-1616-1636.name: Later Jin
later-jin-1616-1636.summary: A Jurchen-led dynasty established in Manchuria in 1616 by Nurhaci, renamed Great Qing in 1636 to begin the Qing dynasty.

yongle-emperor.name: Yongle Emperor
yongle-emperor.summary: Third emperor of the Ming dynasty, reigning 1402 to 1424 after seizing the throne from his nephew; moved the capital to Beijing and sponsored the Yongle Encyclopedia.

ming-treasure-voyages.name: Ming treasure voyages
ming-treasure-voyages.summary: Seven Ming-era naval expeditions (1405–1433) commanded by Admiral Zheng He, reaching as far as India, the Persian Gulf, Arabia and East Africa.

haijin.name: Haijin (Sea Ban)
haijin.summary: A series of Chinese policies restricting private maritime trade during the Ming and early Qing dynasties, first imposed in 1371 to curb piracy and later used to isolate Ming loyalists.

chinggisids.name: Chinggisids
chinggisids.summary: The descendants of Genghis Khan and his wife Börte, who by tradition were considered the only legitimate rulers of the Mongol Empire and its successor states, a rule that lasted until 1847.

northern-yuan.name: Northern Yuan
northern-yuan.summary: Mongol Borjigin dynastic state on the Mongolian Plateau, a rump state formed after the Yuan dynasty's collapse in 1368 and conquered by the Later Jin dynasty in 1635.

nurhaci.name: Nurhaci
nurhaci.summary: Founding khan of the Later Jin dynasty (1559–1626) who united the Jurchen tribes, built the Eight Banners military system, and is credited with creating a Manchu writing script.

wang-yangming.name: Wang Yangming
wang-yangming.summary: Ming dynasty Chinese statesman, general and Neo-Confucian philosopher (1472–1529), regarded as the most important Neo-Confucian thinker after Zhu Xi and founder of the Lu–Wang school of thought.

neo-confucianism.name: Neo-Confucianism
neo-confucianism.summary: A revival of Confucianism as an ethical, social and religious system that dominated Chinese philosophy from the 13th to 19th century, developed under Zhu Xi during the Song dynasty.

joseon.name: Joseon
joseon.summary: A Korean dynastic kingdom founded in 1392 by Taejo, lasting 505 years until 1897, which entrenched Confucian ideals and saw the height of classical Korean culture and science.

afaq-khoja.name: Afaq Khoja
afaq-khoja.summary: A Naqshbandi Sufi leader holding the title Khwaja who also ruled as a political leader in Kashgaria, in present-day southern Xinjiang, also known by his birth name Hidayat Allah.

qi-jingyi.name: Qi Jingyi
qi-jingyi.summary: Chinese Sufi master (1656–1719), also known as Hilal al-Din, who helped spread the Qadiriyya Sufi order among Chinese Muslims.

ma-laichi.name: Ma Laichi
ma-laichi.summary: Chinese Sufi master, around 1681 to 1766, who brought the Khufiyya movement to China and founded the Huasi menhuan, its earliest major Naqshbandi order.

ma-mingxin.name: Ma Mingxin
ma-mingxin.summary: Chinese Sufi master, 1719 to 1781, who founded the Jahriyya order, a branch of Naqshbandi Sufism in China.

qadiri-order.name: Qadiriyya
qadiri-order.summary: A Sunni Sufi order founded by Abdul Qadir Gilani (1077 to 1166), now widespread across South Asia, China, Turkey, and Africa.

confucius.name: Confucius
confucius.summary: Chinese philosopher (c. 551–479 BCE) whose teachings on morality, family loyalty, and social harmony, known as Confucianism, shaped much of Chinese and East Asian culture.

congregation-for-the-evangelization-of-p.name: Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith
congregation-for-the-evangelization-of-p.summary: A Roman Curia body of the Catholic Church, founded in 1622, responsible for missionary work; also known as Propaganda Fide before its 2022 merger.
congregation-for-the-evangelization-of-p.source_title: Congregation for the Evangelization of Peoples

pope-clement-xi.name: Pope Clement XI
pope-clement-xi.summary: Head of the Catholic Church from 1700 to 1721, a patron of arts and science who supported the Vatican Library and archaeological excavations in Rome.

matteo-ricci.name: Matteo Ricci
matteo-ricci.summary: Italian Jesuit missionary (1552–1610) at the Ming court who mastered Chinese and became the first European to enter Beijing's Forbidden City.

shangdi.name: Shangdi
shangdi.summary: The name for the Chinese "Lord Above," the highest deity in classical Chinese theology, rooted in Shang-dynasty worship and still used today in several Chinese religious and philosophical traditions.

jade-emperor.name: Jade Emperor
jade-emperor.summary: A representation of the primordial god in Chinese mythology and folk religion, seen in Taoist theology as assistant to one of the Three Pure Ones.

yongzheng-emperor.name: Yongzheng Emperor
yongzheng-emperor.summary: Fourth emperor of the Qing dynasty, who died in 1735 after a reign known for cracking down on corruption, reforming administration, and creating the Grand Council.

giuseppe-castiglione-jesuit-painter.name: Giuseppe Castiglione
giuseppe-castiglione-jesuit-painter.summary: An Italian Jesuit missionary and painter (1688–1766) who served as court artist to three Qing emperors in China, blending European and Chinese painting styles.

yixing.name: Yixing
yixing.summary: County-level city in Jiangsu, China, known for its traditional clay teapots made from local Yixing clay.

romance-of-the-three-kingdoms.name: Romance of the Three Kingdoms
romance-of-the-three-kingdoms.summary: A 14th-century Chinese historical novel covering events from the decline of the Han dynasty to reunification under the Western Jin in 280, one of the Four Great Classic Novels of Chinese literature.

water-margin.name: Water Margin
water-margin.summary: A Ming-dynasty Chinese novel about 108 outlaws who gather at Mount Liang to rebel against the government, regarded as one of the masterpieces of early vernacular Chinese fiction.

journey-to-the-west.name: Journey to the West
journey-to-the-west.summary: 16th-century Chinese novel attributed to Wu Cheng'en, a fantastical retelling of the monk Xuanzang's 7th-century pilgrimage to India, regarded as one of the great and most popular works of Chinese literature.

jin-ping-mei.name: The Golden Lotus
jin-ping-mei.summary: 16th-century Chinese novel of manners, also known as Jin Ping Mei, published under a pseudonym and noted for its explicit depiction of sexuality.

yixing-ware.name: Yixing ware (zisha)
yixing-ware.summary: Unglazed, typically red or brown stoneware, also called zisha, made from clay near Yixing, China, used for teaware since the Song dynasty and exported to Europe from the 17th century.

dream-of-the-red-chamber.name: Dream of the Red Chamber
dream-of-the-red-chamber.summary: An 18th-century Chinese novel by Cao Xueqin, one of the Four Great Classic Novels, noted for its psychological depth and its portrayal of a family's rise and decline.

yuan-mei.name: Yuan Mei
yuan-mei.summary: A Chinese poet and artist (1716–1797), often paired with Ji Yun as one of his era's leading literary figures.

wuyi-mountains.name: Wuyi Mountains
wuyi-mountains.summary: Mountain range in Fujian province, China, known for producing oolong and black teas such as Da Hong Pao and lapsang souchong, and recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

recipes-from-the-garden-of-contentment.name: Recipes from the Garden of Contentment
recipes-from-the-garden-of-contentment.summary: An 18th-century Chinese work on cooking and gastronomy by Yuan Mei, published in 1792, containing instructions, critiques and recipes for dishes of the period.
recipes-from-the-garden-of-contentment.source_title: Recipes from the Garden of Contentment
